clinicalPearls: A malignant sarcoma of peripheral nerve sheath differentiation, arising sporadically, after radiotherapy, or in association with neurofibromatosis type 1
About half of cases occur in patients with neurofibromatosis type 1, in whom they frequently develop from a pre-existing plexiform neurofibroma
In neurofibromatosis type 1, new or worsening pain, rapid enlargement, or a neurological deficit in a known neurofibroma should raise strong suspicion of malignant transformation
Commonly involves major nerves and nerve plexuses of the trunk and proximal limbs, and can produce motor or sensory deficits along the affected nerve
Molecularly characterised by loss of NF1 and CDKN2A together with inactivation of the PRC2 complex (loss of SUZ12 or EED), reflected in loss of H3K27me3 staining
S100 and SOX10 are often only focally positive, and loss of H3K27 trimethylation on immunohistochemistry aids the diagnosis
Wide surgical excision offers the best chance of control, with radiotherapy for local control and chemotherapy in selected high-grade or advanced cases
Functional imaging can help identify malignant transformation within a plexiform neurofibroma and guide biopsy of the most suspicious area
reference.pathophysiology: Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour is an aggressive sarcoma showing nerve sheath (usually Schwann cell) differentiation. In neurofibromatosis type 1 it typically arises through malignant progression of a plexiform neurofibroma, driven by biallelic loss of the NF1 tumour-suppressor gene, subsequent loss of CDKN2A, and inactivation of the polycomb repressive complex 2 (through SUZ12 or EED mutation). Loss of PRC2 function results in global loss of histone H3 lysine-27 trimethylation, deregulating gene expression and promoting a high-grade phenotype. Sporadic and radiation-associated tumours accumulate analogous alterations, and the resulting cells display variable, often incomplete, Schwannian marker expression.
additionalDifferentials: Cellular or atypical neurofibroma and plexiform neurofibroma
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the primary lesion and involved nerve to define extent and identify features suggesting malignancy
Whole-body functional imaging to detect malignant transformation within plexiform neurofibromas and stage disease
Image-guided biopsy targeting the most metabolically active or suspicious region, with careful tract planning
Immunohistochemistry including S100, SOX10, and H3K27me3 (loss supports the diagnosis)
Assessment for neurofibromatosis type 1 features and, where relevant, genetic evaluation
redFlags: New, persistent, or worsening pain in a known neurofibroma in a patient with neurofibromatosis type 1
Rapid enlargement of a previously stable nerve-associated mass
New or progressive motor or sensory deficit referable to an involved nerve
A deep-seated enlarging mass along a major nerve or plexus
New respiratory symptoms suggesting pulmonary metastases
reference.prognosis: Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour is an aggressive sarcoma with substantial recurrence and metastatic risk; prognosis depends on tumour size, grade, resectability, and setting, and neurofibromatosis type 1-associated and large or incompletely resected tumours generally carry a worse outcome.
pitfalls: Attributing new pain or growth in a neurofibromatosis type 1 patient to a benign neurofibroma and delaying investigation
Relying on S100 positivity, which is often only focal, without additional markers such as loss of H3K27me3
Sampling a benign area of a large plexiform lesion and missing the malignant component
Underestimating the extent of nerve involvement and achieving inadequate margins
Failing to consider prior radiotherapy as a predisposing factor in sporadic-appearing tumours
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: In a patient with neurofibromatosis type 1, rapid growth, increasing pain, or a new neurological deficit in a known neurofibroma should prompt urgent evaluation for malignant transformation
PET FDG avidity and heterogeneity on contrast MRI can help localize the site of transformation within a plexiform neurofibroma and guide biopsy of the most suspicious area
Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy, most tumours are high grade, and weak or focal S100 staining should not be relied on alone since it is also linked to a higher risk of distant metastasis
Loss of H3K27 trimethylation on immunohistochemistry is a useful additional diagnostic marker
Staging should assess the primary site with MRI and screen for distant disease, particularly pulmonary metastases

Complete surgical resection with attention to achieving negative margins is the most important treatment for primary resectable disease, since tumour size and margin status are the factors most consistently tied to survival
Adjuvant radiotherapy is used for local control, particularly with close margins or high grade tumours, noting this tumour type is relatively radioresistant
The role of neoadjuvant chemotherapy for large primary or locally recurrent disease remains controversial and outcomes with chemotherapy have generally been disappointing
Care should be delivered through a multidisciplinary sarcoma team spanning surgical, medical, and clinical oncology

For locally recurrent, unresectable, or metastatic disease, chemotherapy response rates are modest, with better outcomes when an alkylating agent is combined with an anthracycline-based regimen than with an anthracycline alone

Targeted therapy against the Ras/Raf/MAPK pathway activated by NF1 loss has been explored, including a B-Raf-targeting tyrosine kinase inhibitor, but this remains investigational and outcomes with systemic therapy in advanced disease remain poor overall
Metastasectomy can be considered for limited pulmonary metastatic disease in appropriately selected patients
Long-term surveillance for local recurrence and metastasis with clinical review and cross-sectional imaging is required given the substantial recurrence and metastatic risk

In patients with neurofibromatosis type 1, plexiform and atypical neurofibromas should be monitored for signs of transformation, with genetic counselling and family assessment offered, and any suspected malignant transformation should be referred promptly to a specialist sarcoma centre
